head.h1: Shawarma Station Catering in Dubai — What It Costs and How to Book

opening_paragraph: Shawarma station catering in Dubai from myCHEF starts from AED 150 per person — a vetted chef sets up a live spit, carves chicken and meat shawarma to order, and clears everything away. There is a reason the queue typically forms at the spit: the smell, the sizzle and the theatre of the carve turn a buffet line into the busiest corner of the room. You get that show without the mess, the smoke or the washing up. Tell us your date, guest count and venue, we typically reply within 15 minutes during business hours, with an itemised proposal to follow.

replace_in_block.new_heading: What is on a shawarma station menu in Dubai?
new_paragraphs: A typical shawarma station menu dubai centres on two carved meats plus the trimmings that make each wrap. Guests choose from chicken shawarma marinated in garlic, yoghurt and warm spice, and beef or lamb shawarma layered with onion and Middle Eastern seasoning, both carved thin straight off the spit. Around the station we set warm pita and saj breads, garlic toum, tahini, chilli and pickled turnips, tabbouleh, fattoush and hummus, with fries or spiced rice as a filler for hungrier crowds. Vegetarian and vegan carvers, a mixed-grill upgrade and a mezze spread are all available, and the shawarma station food catering dubai line-up flexes for dietary needs on request. Everything is halal by default, which fits most Dubai gatherings, and the full menu is confirmed in writing before your event.

new_paragraphs: A shawarma station suits almost any gathering, from a fifty-guest villa party to a five-hundred-person corporate launch. For weddings and engagements it works beautifully as a late-night station once the plated dinner is done — guests love a hot, hand-carved wrap at midnight. Corporate shawarma station catering dubai teams book it for staff celebrations, ramadan iftars, product launches and exhibition stands, where a live cook and a moving queue create energy on the floor. For home celebrations, birthdays and reunions, shawarma station party catering dubai brings a relaxed, generous, shareable feel that a tray buffet cannot match. Because it is genuinely shawarma station catering for events dubai of every size, we scale the number of spits and carvers to your headcount so nobody waits too long. Larger jobs get more stations and more hands.

add_block.new_heading: The full shawarma station menu, course by course
new_paragraphs: Here is the working list your proposal gets built from, in the order a Dubai grill spread runs: the cold table first, hot pastries while the spit comes up to heat, then the carve, then a centrepiece and dessert. MyCHEF designs the menu and matches the chef to it; the kitchen and the carver cook it. Nothing below is a fixed package — you take a handful of items per section and we cost it against your headcount and venue.
Cold mezze and salads — on the table before anything is carved
This spread does the work while guests arrive and it is the section people photograph. Dubai menus typically publish around twenty and let you choose five to eight.
Hummus: chickpeas blended with tahini, lemon and olive oil (vegan).
Moutabal: smoked aubergine whipped smooth with tahini and yoghurt.
Baba Ghanouj: chopped smoked aubergine with tomato, onion and pomegranate molasses (vegan).
Tabbouleh: parsley-led, with bulgur, tomato, mint and a heavy hand of lemon (vegan).
Fattoush: chopped garden salad with sumac dressing and crisp fried bread (vegan).
Rocca Salad with Onion & Tomato: peppery rocket, red onion and tomato in a lemon dressing.
Rocca with Feta Cheese: the same rocket base with salty feta crumbled through it.
Vine Leaves (Warak Enab): vine leaves rolled around rice, tomato and herbs (vegan).
Labneh with Garlic: strained yoghurt beaten with garlic and flooded with olive oil.
Muhammara: red pepper and walnut dip sharpened with pomegranate molasses — nut-heavy, so flag it.
Shanklish: aged cheese rolled in thyme and served with tomato and onion.
Hindbeh: chicory wilted in olive oil under a lid of crisp fried onion.
Quinoa Tabouleh: the parsley salad rebuilt on quinoa instead of bulgur.
Lentil Tabouleh: green lentils, herbs and lemon — the heavier of the two tabboulehs.
Freekeh Salad: smoked green wheat with herbs and a lemon dressing.
Beetroot Salad: roasted beetroot with tahini or yoghurt and toasted seeds.
Kale & Quinoa: the salad that holds up longest on an outdoor table in Dubai.
Green Apple Coleslaw: shredded cabbage and green apple, cut sharper than a creamy slaw.
Potato Salad: dressed while the potatoes are still warm, so it takes the seasoning.
Three Bean Salad: mixed beans in a vinaigrette, and one of the few cold items that is not bread-led.
Mixed Olives with Pickles: green and black olives alongside Arabic pickles.
Fresh Vegetable Platter: raw crudités cut wide enough to scoop the dips.
Pickled Cucumber: house pickles, sharp enough to reset the palate between wraps.
Hot appetisers and pastries — while the spit comes up to heat
A shawarma spit needs time on the burner before the outer layer is ready to shave. These fill that gap.
Fried Kebbe: bulgur shells stuffed with spiced minced meat and pine nuts, fried to order.
Cheese Sambousek: folded pastry filled with white cheese.
Meat Sambousek: the same pastry filled with minced meat and onion.
Spinach Fatayer: triangular baked pastry with spinach, lemon and sumac.
Cheese Rolls: crisp rolled pastry, served straight out of the fryer.
Falafel: fried chickpea and herb patties, served with tahini (vegan).
Spiced Potato with Coriander: cubed potato tossed hot with coriander, garlic and chilli (vegan).
Makanek: small Lebanese sausages finished with lemon.
Sujouk: spiced dried sausage, sliced and pan-crisped.
Fried Chicken Liver: cooked hard and fast with pomegranate molasses.
Chicken Wings: marinated and fried, then tossed with garlic.
Hummus Fatteh: hummus layered over fried bread with yoghurt and toasted nuts.
Eggplant Fatteh: the same layered dish built on fried aubergine.
Fried Calamari: served with tartare or a lemon and garlic dip.
Kofta Balls with Pomegranate: minced meat balls glazed in pomegranate molasses.
Mousakhan Rolls: sumac chicken and onion rolled in flatbread and baked.
Mini Lahem Beajine: the small open meat pastry, Trabolsi or Baalbaki style.
Arayes Kafta: bread stuffed with spiced minced meat and pressed onto the grill until crisp.
The spits themselves

Chicken and beef stack on separate vertical rotisseries, so a menu offering both means two units on the station, not one. The chicken is layered with garlic, yoghurt and warm spice; the beef or lamb is built with onion, fat and Middle Eastern seasoning so it bastes itself as it turns. Stations are sold across Dubai by the weight loaded onto the spit, and 10 kg is the standard unit. A wagyu shawarma spit is the upgrade where the brief is a premium one. Where the spit can stand is worth settling early, and the fuel decides it. A gas spit is an outdoor villa setup and it does not go on a Dubai rooftop at all: the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code bars LPG cylinders from any roof or terrace and keeps them at ground level, and above 90 m no LPG reaches the roof even on a piped supply, so a roof takes the electric spit and the same cone. In the desert the gas spit runs normally, with the cylinders in a shaded, ventilated store, out of the direct sun. In a tower apartment the cylinder is the problem rather than the spit — no LPG cylinder may be brought into the building or the unit — so the electric vertical spit is the version that goes up in the lift. On a yacht neither runs: no additional gas cylinder may be brought aboard under the marina rules, so the cone is cooked in the licensed partner kitchen and carved live on deck, which is the part guests watch.
Live shawarma station, chicken: layered with garlic, yoghurt and warm spice, shaved to order.
Live shawarma station, beef or lamb: built with onion, fat and Middle Eastern seasoning so it bastes itself as it turns.
Wagyu shawarma spit: the upgrade where the brief is a premium one.
Served the way it is served here: Arabic bread, French fries, garlic paste, fresh tomato, pickles and sliced lettuce, with tahini and chilli alongside.
Off the mangal beside the spit — Arabic mashawi

Most hosts pair the carve with charcoal skewers so there is something coming off two fires at once. Charcoal is the part that depends on where you are. At a villa the answer is yes: coals run outdoors on your own plot — garden or driveway, firm level base — but not inside, because Dubai Municipality's barbecue guidance says plainly not to light coal in an enclosed space or indoors. In an apartment it is a flat no; Emaar's vertical-community rules bar barbecues, grills or cooking equipment of any kind from balconies and terraces, whatever the fuel. In the desert coals are straightforwardly fine in the open air and banned inside a tent or an enclosed majlis, so the mangal stands outside it, and every coal and all the ash leave with the catering team — Dubai Municipality enforces that against the caterer, not the host. On a rooftop charcoal is permitted but extracted: under any covered section it has to sit beneath a grease-rated hood with suppression, so an open unhooded roof deck is where it has to change. Where charcoal is not on, the same skewers come off a gas or electric grill and the char is built in the licensed partner kitchen — every item below stays on the menu.
Shish Tawouk: marinated chicken cubes on a skewer, the most-ordered item on any Dubai grill.
Lamb Kabab: minced lamb pressed onto the skewer and cooked over coals.
Kabab Khoush Khash: the same kebab built with tomato and chilli, for a spicier board.
Kabab Orfali: Aleppo-style kebab with parsley and pepper through the mince.
Lamb Chops: cutlets grilled hard and fast, left pink unless you say otherwise.
Lamb Meat Cubes: cubed lamb skewered between onion and pepper.
Grilled Meat (Lahem Meshwi): the plain charcoal skewer, seasoning and fire only.
Kafta: minced meat with parsley and onion, moulded by hand onto the skewer.
Chicken Kafta: the same preparation built on minced chicken.
Arayes: Arabic bread stuffed with spiced mince, grilled until the outside crisps.
Whole Boneless Chicken: butterflied, grilled flat and cut at the station.
Mixed Grill with Tawouk: a shared platter of tawouk, kafta and lamb cubes.
Masbaha with Pine Nuts: warm whole chickpeas in tahini under toasted pine nuts — nut-heavy.
Grilled Tomato & Onion: the standard skewer garnish, charred beside the meat.
Makanek: Lebanese sausages, this time straight off the coals.
Sujouk: spiced sausage grilled until the edges catch.
Lamb Loin: the leaner premium cut off the mangal.
Desi grill, when the room briefs it that way

Subcontinental guests brief by ratio — two veg to three non-veg mains — not by dish, and it is worth saying so up front. Naan comes off a tandoor set beside the spit. The tandoor goes to villa gardens and driveways, outdoors and at ground level; on a rooftop it follows its fuel and its extraction, which means a charcoal tandoor under the venue's extracted cooking line and no gas one, and in the desert it wants a trailer or platform base, because soft sand will not hold a fired clay body level. On a yacht or an apartment balcony it does not go at all. Where it cannot travel, the same naan, kulcha and tikka are baked in the licensed partner kitchen and finished hot on site, which is how most of this section is served anyway.
Seekh Kebab: minced meat rolled onto a flat skewer for the tandoor.
Chicken Seekh Kebab: the chicken version, milder and quicker to cook.
Beef Seekh Kebab: the beef version, spiced heavier.
Chapli Kebab: the flat Peshawari patty, with tomato, coriander and crushed spice.
Tikka Boti: marinated meat cubes cooked in the tandoor.
Malai Boti: cream-and-cheese marinated chicken, the mild end of the board.
Chicken Tikka: yoghurt and spice marinade, cooked until the edges char.
Fish Tikka: firm white fish given the same marinade and a much shorter cook.
Paneer Tikka: pressed Indian cheese skewered with peppers and onion (vegetarian).
Tandoori Vegetables: cauliflower, mushroom and pepper cooked in the tandoor.
Mutton Ribs: marinated long, then finished over fire.
Chicken Karahi: the accompanying curry, cooked down in a wok-style pan.
Mutton Biryani: the accompanying rice, layered with mutton and whole spice.
Continental and steakhouse cuts
This is usually what separates a standard spread from a premium one, and cut and provenance say more than any adjective.
Ribeye Steaks: grilled to order and rested before they are sliced.
Tomahawk Steak: with rosemary and thyme gremolata, truffle butter, roast baby potatoes and vegetables.
Black Onyx Tomahawk: the graded Australian version of the same cut.
Wagyu Skirt Steak: fast over high heat, then sliced against the grain.
Angus Short Rib: cooked long and finished on the grill.
Wagyu Beef Cheeks: braised until they give — the richest thing on the board.
Picanha: rump cap grilled fat-side down, Brazilian style.
Argentinian Ribeye: the imported ribeye, cooked over open coals.
Spiced Chicken Legs: marinated legs cooked slow enough to stay juicy.
Honey Glazed Chicken Wings: glazed at the end so the sugar does not burn.
Beef Chorizo: grilled whole and sliced at the station.
Schubling and Cheese Knacker: two German-style sausages for a mixed board.
Brisket Sliders: on soft potato buns with truffle aioli, caramelised onions, pickles and parmesan.
Beef and Chicken Sliders: the standard slider pair, built to order in front of guests.
Low and slow, if you want the smokehouse register too

A different fire and a different chef from the mangal, sold by weight or as a feast, not per item. Pork does not appear on a Dubai menu, so the pulled meat here is lamb. The smoker is the least portable thing on this page: solid fuel, a burn measured in hours and a continuous plume, so it belongs outdoors on a villa plot, or at a desert camp, where the fuel pile stays well clear of the tent fabric and the burn has to start before guests arrive, so myCHEF books an earlier site-access window than the camp's standard one. It does not go on an apartment balcony or aboard a boat. Everything listed here can instead be smoked overnight in the licensed partner kitchen and carved live at the station, which is how brisket and pastrami reach a Dubai event in practice.
Prime Brisket: rubbed, smoked overnight and sliced to order.
Salt and pepper brisket: the Texas register — seasoning and smoke, nothing else.
Smoked Wagyu Brisket: the marbled upgrade of the same cut.
Wagyu Smoked Beef Ribs: sold by the rib and cut at the board.
Beef Ribs: the standard smoked rib, sold by weight.
Pastrami: brined, spiced, smoked and sliced thin.
Pulled Lamb: shredded slow-cooked lamb, which is how this market does pulled meat.
Lamb Leg: smoked whole, then carved at the station.
Smoked Chicken: whole birds smoked and jointed.
Beef Chorizo: warmed through on the smoker and sliced.
Duck: smoked, glazed and carved to order.
Served with: Mandi Rice, Coleslaw, Potato Salad, Three Bean Salad and potato buns.
Grilled seafood — the usual upgrade
On competitor menus this is the paid step that moves a package to its top tier, and it is the section most hosts under-order.
Grilled Jumbo Shrimp: shell on, garlic and lemon, cooked in minutes.
Tiger Prawn Skewers: two or three prawns to a skewer so they come off the fire together.
Grilled Hammour Fillet: the local white fish, grilled plain.
BBQ Hammour: the same fish with a heavier marinade and more char.
Salmon Fillet: grilled skin-side down and lifted while it is still translucent inside.
Smoked Ocean Trout: cold-smoked and sliced, served from the cold table.
Fried Calamari: crisp, with lemon and a garlic dip.
Octopus Provencal: braised soft, then finished with tomato, olives and capers.
Lobster Tail Tacos: the top-tier item, assembled to order.
Skewers Salmon: cubed salmon on the skewer for a mixed seafood platter.
Skewers Seafood: prawn, fish and calamari on one stick.
Fish Sayadieh: fish over spiced onion rice, Levantine style.
Herb Marinated Fish: whole or filleted, marinated green and grilled.
Vegetarian and vegan off the grill — a section, not a footnote

These get their own space on the fire and their own utensils. Nothing here is scraped onto a corner of the meat grill. The robata skewers in this list are charcoal like the mangal, so they take the same answer: a villa garden yes, an apartment balcony no, and on a rooftop or in the desert the counter decides it, not the coals — the robata runs open-sided on desert ground, and on a roof it needs its own duct straight to the outside air, not one shared with the building's ventilation. Where coals are refused the same skewers run on an electric yakitori griddle, which keeps the counter and the to-order service the format is sold on.
Grilled Halloumi: scored and grilled until it squeaks, finished with lemon.
Paneer Tikka: the tandoor version, on its own skewers.
BBQ Corn Cob: charred on the grill and rolled in butter and spice.
Grilled Vegetables: courgette, aubergine, pepper and onion, dressed warm.
Vegetable Skewers: the same vegetables built onto sticks for a standing crowd.
Marinated Mushrooms: marinated first so they do not dry out over coals.
Grilled Peppers: blistered whole, then peeled and dressed with olive oil.
Zucchini and Eggplant skewers: cut thick so they hold together on the fire.
Asparagus and Artichoke skewers: the premium vegetarian skewer.
Shiitake Mushroom skewers: from the robata register, grilled dry.
Negima spring onion skewers: charred whole spring onion, sweet once it softens.
Vegetarian Burgers: cooked on their own section of the grill.
Falafel: fried to order beside the station, not made ahead (vegan).
Sauteed Vegetables: the hot vegetable side for a buffet line.
The centrepiece
A whole roast carved beside the spits is what gives an event its photograph. One lamb is typically sized to around 30 guests; we put the exact count in your proposal so you are not guessing.
Full Roasted Lamb Station: the whole animal carved in front of guests, typically sized to around 30 people.
Lamb Roasting Station: 13 kg Australian lamb turned whole.
Whole or Half Lamb: on an Oriental, Biryani or Friki rice bed.
Lamb Leg: the same three rice beds, sized for a smaller room.
Lamb Ouzi: lamb over spiced rice, wrapped and baked.
Mansaf Kharouf: lamb with a yoghurt sauce, served over rice.
Mutton Ra'an: the whole marinated leg, and the Desi answer to a centrepiece.
Roasted Baby Leg of Lamb: the smaller carve for a villa dinner.
Whole Turkey with Oriental Rice: the seasonal alternative to lamb.
Slow-roasted beef ribeye: carved to order beside the spits.
Rice, staples and hot sides
A rice is non-negotiable on any Arabic or Desi spread, and it is the thing that stops a shawarma queue turning into a second dinner.
White Basmati Rice: the plain base every other dish is served over.
Biryani Rice: layered with whole spice and fried onion.
Chicken Biryani: the full dish, not the rice alone.
Chicken or Lamb Kabseh: Gulf spiced rice cooked with the meat in it.
Chicken Freekeh: smoked green wheat cooked like a rice, with chicken through it.
Moghrabieh with Meat and Chicken: Lebanese pearl couscous in a caraway broth.
Arabic Rice: vermicelli rice topped with toasted nuts.
Roasted Potatoes: cut large and roasted hard.
Country Potato: skin-on wedges with a dry spice rub.
Battat Fries: Arabic-style fries served hot to the wrap station.
Cajun sweet potato fries: oven-baked, and the better match for smoked meat.
Herbed Couscous: the lighter grain option on a grill spread.
Fasolia Bil Zeit: green beans stewed in olive oil and tomato (vegan).
Bamieh Bil Zeit: okra cooked the same way (vegan).
Grilled Tomato & Onion: charred whole, and served as a side, not a garnish.
Breads and the saj

Bread arrives as a basket by default. A live saj or Arabic bread oven is the upgrade, and the smell of it carries as far across a room as the spit does. A gas saj is a plain yes outdoors at a villa; an electric saj is the one that works in a tower apartment, where no cylinder may be brought into the building. On a yacht the saj stays ashore, because no additional gas cylinder comes aboard, and the manakeesh are baked in the licensed partner kitchen and finished warm on deck.
Fresh Arabic Bread: the default basket, warmed at the station.
Fresh-baked pita: baked on site where the venue allows an oven.
Kaak Bread: the sesame-crusted Levantine bread.
Potato Bun: soft buns for the sliders and pulled lamb.
Naan: off the tandoor set beside the spit.
Live saj station: Zaatar, Cheese, Kishek and Lahem Beajine made to order on the dome.
Manakeesh: Zaatar, Cheese, Meat, Turkey & Cheese, or Nutella.
Live Arabic bread oven: bread pulled hot in front of guests, and the smell carries as far as the spit.
Sauces and relishes, named one by one
Weak menus write “signature sauces&rdquo. Here is what is in the pots.
Garlic sauce (toum): whipped garlic emulsion, the one nobody skips.
Tahini: sesame paste loosened with lemon and water.
Pickled turnips: the pink pickle that belongs in the wrap.
House-made tomato relish: chopped and dressed, not cooked down.
Beetroot relish: sweet and sharp against smoked meat.
Chimichurri: parsley, garlic, oregano and vinegar for the steakhouse cuts.
Gremolata: lemon zest, parsley and garlic, cut fresh at the station.
Creamy BBQ: the mild sauce for a mixed crowd.
Peach habanero BBQ sauce: sweet first, hot afterwards.
Marmalade smoked tonkatsu BBQ sauce: dark, sweet and smoky, built for brisket.
Maple syrup, chilli, pineapple and vanilla relish: the sweet relish on the smokehouse board.
Yoghurt with Cucumber & Mint: the cooling dip beside the spice.
Mustard: for the sausages and the sliders.
Dessert
Arabic first, western alongside, and a live kunafa pan if you want a second piece of theatre once the carving stops.
Cheese Kunafa: shredded pastry over stretchy cheese, soaked in syrup and served hot from a live pan.
Halawet El Jibben: sweet cheese rolls filled with ashta and dressed with syrup.
Othmalieh: crisp kunafa pastry layered with cheese or kashta.
Umm Ali: the Egyptian bread pudding, baked with milk and nuts.
Znood El Sit: fried pastry fingers filled with cream.
Mafroukeh: semolina and ashta under pistachio — nut-heavy.
Maamoul Bil Ashta: date or nut pastry served with clotted cream.
Mixed Baklawa: the assorted tray, and one of the nuttiest items on the menu.
Mohalabieh: milk pudding set soft, with orange blossom.
Riz Bel Halib: rice pudding, served cold.
Katayef Kashta: folded pancakes filled with cream.
Crème Caramel: the western set custard that clears the table fastest.
Assorted Mini Cakes: the small western tray for a mixed room.
Cheesecake: baked or set, cut into squares for a buffet.
Tiramisu: served in trays or individual glasses.
Black Forest: chocolate, cream and cherry, cut at the table.
Macarons: the colour on the dessert table.
Fresh Fruit Salad: cut on the day, and the thing half the room takes.
Sliced Fruit Platter: watermelon, melon and pineapple, cut large.
The same station shrunk to canapés
For a standing reception the carve becomes finger food, priced per piece with twelve pieces the usual minimum per variety.
Mini Shawarma: a single-bite version of the carve, wrapped tight.
Mini Beef or Chicken Shawarma Wrap: the same wrap in either meat.
Chicken Shawarma Moneybags: shawarma tied into a pastry purse.
Shawarma Mini Brioche Sandwich: carved meat in a soft brioche roll.
Mini Shish Taouk Brochette: a two-bite chicken skewer.
Mini Kafta: the kebab shrunk to canapé size.
Mini Grilled Meat: a single skewered cube off the mangal.
Mini Lamb Kebab Skewers: served with garlic sauce on the side.
Mini Falafel Wrap: the vegan option on the tray, not an afterthought.
Mini Kofta Sandwich: kofta in a small soft roll.
Kebbeh Balls: stuffed with hummus, moutabal or tabbouleh and topped with pomegranate.
Where the dietary lines fall

Halal is the baseline across every item above, which is table stakes in Dubai and not a selling point. Vegetarian is well served here and gets its own grill block. Genuinely vegan as served: Baba Ghanouj, Hummus, Stuffed Vine Leaves, Fattoush, Tabbouleh, Falafel and the Mini Falafel Wrap. Gluten-free is the honest weak spot — this spread is bread-led, so a gluten-free guest needs deliberate substitution, and we plan it into the order. Dairy-free needs the same care, because labneh, shanklish, halloumi and kunafa are all dairy-central. Nuts are the disclosure gap nobody in this market handles well: baklawa, mafroukeh, muhammara and the pine-nut garnishes are nut-heavy, so flag allergies when you brief us and we will build the sections around them.
Reading this as a price list

Treat the menu above as a list to choose from, not a set package, because the format you pick moves the number more than the dishes do. Delivered and set out as a spread, the volume tiers start at AED 90 per person for a working lunch and AED 120 for a standard event buffet. The live shawarma station itself — spit, carver and the bread, sauces and salads around it — is quoted from AED 150 per person, which is the premium buffet and live-station tier. A full private-chef dinner, plated and served course by course, is a different product again at AED 700 to AED 950 per person, and it is not what most people booking a station are after. Volume formats run from 10 guests, a station or buffet from 20, with a minimum order value of AED 900. Cheap shawarma catering in this city usually shows up in the meat, not the invoice, so ask any quote what goes on the spit before you compare the numbers.

new_paragraphs: A single station needs roughly a three-by-two-metre footprint with a nearby power point or gas feed, and the fuel decides where it can stand. A gas spit is an outdoor setup on a villa's own plot, at ground level and roughly three metres clear of windows, AC intakes and exit routes, because a turning cone drips fat and throws grease-laden vapour a domestic room is not built to take. An electric spit is the one that works indoors and in a tower apartment, where no cylinder may be brought into the building at all — same carve, same queue, no cylinder. We confirm access, timing and the venue's own rules in advance, and coordinate with your planner or building management where needed. On dietary needs, every menu is halal, and we cater nut-free, gluten-free and vegetarian guests when you flag them — tell us your numbers and we build the station around them. add_block.new_heading: How many spits does your headcount need?
new_paragraphs: This is the question that decides both the price and whether anyone queues. One spit with one carver holds a room of about 100 comfortably across a two-hour service, because the limit is not the meat on the spit but how fast one pair of hands can shave, fill and pass a wrap. At 200 guests a second spit stops the line forming; at 300 to 500 you are into three or four, usually split across two points in the room so the crowd divides itself. Standing receptions eat faster than seated ones, and a late-night station after a plated dinner runs at maybe half the rate of a station that is the whole meal, so tell us which it is. Each spit needs its own three-by-two-metre footprint and its own power or gas feed, which is normally the real constraint in an apartment or on a rooftop rather than anything to do with the food.
